info.bio:
Franz Ferdinand es una banda de rock formada en Glasgow (Escocia) en 2001.

El grupo escocés toma su nombre del archiduque austrohúngaro Francisco Fernando (Franz Ferdinand en alemán) cuyo asesinato fue la excusa final que llevaría a la Iª Guerra Mundial, la llamada Gran Guerra. 

A finales de 2001, Bob estaba sentado en la cocina de Alex. Alex justo había recibido un bajo de parte de su amigo Mick Cooke (Belle & Sebastian), a condición que hiciera "algo útil" con él.

scenes.name: Renacimiento neopostpunk
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Con el nuevo milenio, hipsters hastiados de las discotecas buscan tensión en lugar de catarsis: reediciones de Cabaret Voltaire, Throbbing Gristle, 23 Skidoo, ESG, DNA y Scritti Politti, clubes de punk funk y electropop, reuniones de Gang of Four y Mission of Burma, las películas 24 Hour Party People y Control, y bandas como The Rapture, LCD Soundsystem, Franz Ferdinand, Interpol, Liars, !!!, Wolf Eyes y Bloc Party. Dominan las inflexiones de la militancia postpunk, pero no su compromiso: lo más valioso de aquella época era su fe en el cambio, «que la música podía importar tanto».

podcast.title: Alt Rock Resurgence of 2004
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand was named as one of the new and exciting bands contributing to the resurgence of Alt Rock by 2004. "By 2004, Alt Rock was back with all kinds of new exciting bands that was Franz Ferdinand and Modest Mouse and the Killers and Billy Towns and the Stills and Jet, the Ye-Yaz and Hot Hot Heat."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 500th Show!

podcast.title: Artsy Scottish Approach (Pre-2005)
podcast.body: The band's "artsy Scottish approach was getting written up everywhere" by spring 2005, contributing to their hit albums and the overall rock revival. "Franz Ferdinand's artsy Scottish approach was getting written up everywhere."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Alt Rock Chapter: 14

podcast.title: "The Chateau" Rehearsal Space
podcast.body: The band's initial rehearsal space was an abandoned warehouse they creatively named "The Chateau." This venue also hosted their gigs and art events, but it was eventually raided by the police, forcing them to relocate. "That track came together in the rehearsal space, which was an abandoned warehouse that they called the Chateau, a little artistic irony there."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Alex Kapranos's Activities During Band Break
podcast.body: During the band's break after touring in late 2006, Alex Kapranos went to Vancouver to produce The Cribs' album and recorded his own album with a friend named Danny, released by Domino Records under the character name Victoria and Albert. The band regrouped in February 2007. "I went to Vancouver and produced the crib's last record. They went to New York and mixed that. I recorded an album, I hear my friend Danny, that's a character, which Domino put out this year actually."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Alex Kapranos's Food Writing
podcast.body: Alex Kapranos began writing about food for The Guardian after an editor approached him. Despite initial skepticism about his qualifications as a musician, his past experience as a chef and the opportunity to travel globally, trying unusual foods like deep-fried locusts and bulls' testicles, provided a unique perspective. He appreciated the "naivety" his lack of a food critic's vocabulary brought to his writing. "The idea was my idea, I've got to be totally honest about that, it was one of the editors at the Guardian, approached me and said, what do you want to write about food and my immediate reaction was like, well of course I can't write about food, I'm a guy in a band, I don't know anything about it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Artwork Inspired by Cindy Sherman and Weegee
podcast.body: For the artwork of their third album, Tonight, Franz Ferdinand's visual imagery shifted to a "nighttime record" theme, inspired by photographers Cindy Sherman and Weegee. They created a series of improvised nighttime "crime scenes," similar to Sherman's untitled film stills and Weegee's flash-bulb crime scene photography, inviting fans to imagine the narrative. "And they're based around the ideas of two photographers, Cindy Sherman and Ouija."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Backmasking in Digital Era
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand is listed among artists who have utilized backward messages, particularly in the period following the late 1990s and early 2000s when digital sound editing software made the practice more accessible. "Back, cake, cold play, M&M, Fransford Nand, Lincoln Park, Marilyn Manson, Moby Soundgarden Tool, 21 Pilots, and a ton more."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Rock Explainer 5

podcast.title: Band Name Origin - Archduke Franz Ferdinand
podcast.body: The band's name was chosen by its artsy members, who viewed it as a "mission." It refers to Archduke Franz Ferdinand, a member of the Austro-Hungarian Royal Family whose assassination on June 28, 1914, in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip triggered World War I, marking the beginning of the 20th century's widespread carnage. The band found the name appealing for its sound, rhythm, and historical significance, aspiring for their music to have a similar pivotal impact. "But also the theory behind the name was that he was this guy and when he was shot everything turned on that moment, nothing was quite the same afterwards."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Death Threat Incident
podcast.body: Alex Kapranos recounted receiving a death threat from someone who claimed to be a "star one" and threatened to murder the band. "only did get a death threat once, didn't they remember? Like some guy said he was going to come and murder us because he was a, I don't know they had good stuff."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Declared Influence
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand is among a partial list of artists and bands who have publicly stated that they have been influenced by Joy Division in some way. "You too, arcade fire, smashing pumpkins, nine inch nails, to pesh mode, sisters of mercy, ministry, chain addiction, the smiths, Bjork, Jesus and Marychain, Moby, primal scream, the Charlotains, Interpol, editors, white lies, Frans Ferdinand. I could go on, but I think you get the point."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?

podcast.title: Early Band Formation and Delays
podcast.body: The band members, Alex Kapranos, Paul Thompson, Bob Hardy, and Nick McCarthy, played in various bands in Glasgow during the 1990s before forming Franz Ferdinand. There was confusion regarding the band's exact formation and first rehearsal dates, with Alex initially suggesting January 2002 or April 2003 for the first show, while Paul insisted it was 2002, citing the recording of their first album in summer 2003 after a year of playing together. "First show, I think, was in April 2003. No, I was 2002."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Encounters with Archduke's Descendants
podcast.body: The band has met descendants of Archduke Franz Ferdinand who were curious to meet them. In one instance at a show in Vienna, two children, identified by local papers as his great-great-grandchildren, were asked to pose with the band while holding an etching of the Archduke's assassination, which Alex Kapranos found morbid. "The weirdest one was when we played in Vienna one time and there were these two kids who came down to the show and the local papers there as well, they were saying, right, okay now we're going to pose to the band and one of the kids to hold this etching of the assassination of the Archduke."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: John Varvatos Ad Campaign
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand's "slim, stylish look" attracted fashion designer John Varvatos, who signed them to front his 2009 ad campaign. This collaboration meant that Alex Kapranos's new wardrobe would be featured extensively in fashion magazines. "Their slim, stylish look caught the eye of designer John Vervardo's. They were signed to front his 2009 ad campaign."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Musical Influences
podcast.body: All members of Franz Ferdinand admired the spiky, jittery, stop-start music of the 1970s, citing influences from Joy Division, The Fall, Blondie, The Stranglers, and Gang of Four. Their music managed to sound fresh despite being inspired by these earlier sounds. "Everybody in the band had a fondness for that spiky, jittery, stop-start stuff in the 1970s. Joy Division in the fall, Blondie, the Stranglers, Gang of Four."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Alt Rock Revivals Part 5: New Wave

podcast.title: Part of New Rock Wave
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand was one of several groups that emerged as part of the new wave of Rock Revival music. They also achieved significant fame through the internet and, like others, gradually integrated into the standards of the record industry. "Tenemos casos como casabian que también se hicieron muy famosos gracias a Internet, tenemos a transferinante que son grupos que yo creo que es, a pesar de que son muy buenos, han ido entrando poco a poco más en los estándares de la industria discográfica."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: Arctic Monkeys: Cómo nació un mito.

podcast.title: Physical Media Philosophy
podcast.body: Alex Kapranos views records and CDs as containers for music, acknowledging that the music itself is transferable online. He believes that to sell physical containers, they must be desirable, appealing particularly to "vinyl nuts" who demonstrate devotion to music by purchasing and actively listening to vinyl. He differentiates sound quality: vinyl is like cinema, CD is like HDTV, and MP3 is like YouTube. "All the record is or a CD is it's a container for the music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Pioneers of the Indie Rock Revival (Early 2000s)
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand were among the "new, sharp clever bands" that emerged during the Indie Rock Revival or Post-Punk Revival period around 2000-2001. This movement was a refurbished version of old-school early alt-rock, garage rock, and punk styles. "We gave us new, sharp clever bands like the strokes and the hives, the yay-yaz, friends ferdinand, interpool, and the arctic monkeys."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The 100 Greatest Rock Moments of the Millennium So Far - Part 2: (90-81)

podcast.title: Pioneers of the Indie Rock Revival (Early 2000s)

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Dreampop - A History

podcast.title: Repetitive Trajectory in Later Work
podcast.body: As part of the early 2000s rock revival generation, Franz Ferdinand also experienced a period where their later albums became quite repetitive, failing to offer significant new contributions. This situation reflects a common challenge for bands of their generation who struggle to evolve beyond their initial comfort zones. "Cuando vemos los últimos discos que había hecho Franfernan, vemos que los pobres también han entrado en una situación bastante repetitiva en la que ya no aportaban demasiado."

srcs.source: Music Radar Clan
srcs.episode: ARCTIC MONKEYS - Tranquility Base Hotel & Casino. Por qué tiene más sentido del que parece

podcast.title: Role in Bloc Party's Breakthrough
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand's singer, Alex Kapranos, played an unwitting role in Bloc Party's big break when Kele Okereke handed him a demo tape at a show around 2003. "Block Party got their big break when Kelly went to a France Ferdinand show and gave a tape to singer Alex Capranos. That would be about 2003."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Diversity Show 2021

podcast.title: Soviet Technology Experimentation
podcast.body: For their third album, the band experimented with old Soviet technology, specifically Polyvox synthesizers, to achieve a distinctive sound. Alex Kapranos compared these instruments to Lomo cameras or Octavia microphones, noting that they were reverse-engineered versions of Western technology (like Moog synthesizers or Leica cameras), which, while "kind of wrong," produced a "kind of good" and cool sound, characterized by aggressive filters. "One of the things the band experimented with for this record was some old Soviet technology."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Three and a Half Million Records Sold
podcast.body: Following the success of their first two albums, Franz Ferdinand sold a total of three and a half million records, a significant achievement that afforded them the luxury of taking more time to record their third album. "That's what happens when you sell three and a half million records. You get to take your time."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Unconventional Song Structures
podcast.body: Franz Ferdinand is known for experimenting with tempo changes and unconventional song structures, a characteristic Alex Kapranos attributes to a desire for bravery and experimentation in their music. He noted that their approach to "Take Me Out," with its contrasting fast verses and slow choruses, arose from a need to make both sections work effectively while maintaining a strong emphasis on melody within an experimental framework. "I guess it's being brave enough to use an unconventional song structure, you know, a laylite, sort of being a little bit experimental."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Franz Ferdinand: In Their Own Words

podcast.title: Victorian Jail Rehearsal Space
podcast.body: Following a police raid on their previous rehearsal space, "The Chateau," the band moved their operations to a building that had once served as an old Victorian jail. This move continued their pattern of choosing ironically artsy locations for their creative endeavors. "The cops weren't so sympathetic though. They raided the place, necessitating a move to a building that was once an old Victorian jail."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Influence on Other Bands
xref.body: The Strokes, particularly with their debut album "Is This It," profoundly influenced many bands that followed, making them one of the most important bands of the 2000s. Kings of Leon learned to play by emulating "Is This It." The Killers, after hearing the album, reportedly scrapped all their existing material except for "Mr. Brightside" and restarted, with elements of The Strokes' construction and recording audible in their music. Other bands like Arctic Monkeys, Franz Ferdinand, and LCD Sound System also credit The Strokes as an influence. "If it wasn't for the Strokes, it's possible that the Indy Rock Garage Rock Revival that took hold in New York City in the early 2000s wouldn't have grown the way it did."
